+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Azra Gambit - Chapter Three: An Invitation** Arthur kept adjusting his collar. It was not that the collar was too tight. It was precisely his size, measured that morning by a silent Antarean orderly with a tape and a disapproving frown. It was a soft, dark fabric that the orderly had called *terrene wool*, which Arthur, who had not worn anything but synthetics and patched canvas since he was twenty-two, found absurdly warm. He tugged at it again. The gesture was compulsive. The transfer vessel was too quiet. That was the other thing. It was an Antares cutter, a Hermes-class high-orbital shuttle, all smooth retrofuturist lines and brushed aluminum bulkheads that belonged in a newsreel from twenty years ago. No exposed ductwork, no rattle of the recyclers. The acceleration was a steady, polite 1-g, provided by a grav-plate deck that hummed beneath his polished shoes. Through the single broad viewport, Mars fell away beneath them — not the romantic red disc of the old posters, but the real Mars: a scabbed, ochre sphere latticed with the pale scars of strip mines and the domed blisters of the Colonial settlements. His settlement, New Elysium, was already invisible. His claim, Plot 87-B, with its miraculous, impossible Azra reading, was a speck of dust on a speck of dust. He wondered, with the slow, logical dread of an engineer watching a pressure gauge climb into the red, just what he had gotten involved in. "It itches, doesn't it?" said the officer opposite him. Arthur startled. The man had not spoken for twenty minutes. He wore the charcoal-grey of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Diplomatic in name only — everyone on Mars knew that. On his breast was the insignia: a seven-pointed silver starburst on a field of black, the star Antares itself, rendered with geometric precision. The man was young, his hair cut brutally short, his face pleasant and entirely unreadable. Two more like him stood by the hatch, rifles held with that peculiar Antarean politeness — not pointed, but very much present. "It does," Arthur said. "I'm not used to formal attire. I was instructed to wear it." "Yes. The Prefect prefers formality. It helps one remember that civilization is a matter of manners." The officer smiled. "You are Arthur Neegan, Mining Engineer, First Generation. Born in Sheffield, emigrated at age nineteen on the Colonial Indenture Waiver. Plot 87-B. You filed a Geiger anomaly report at 08:14 yesterday. Azra content estimated at four hundred tons. Is that correct?" Arthur's hand went to his collar again and he forced it down to the armrest. "The reading was preliminary. My rig is old. A Scintrex-6, you know. It could be a miscalibration." "Of course," the officer said agreeably. "And yet within six hours, Helion-Murray offered you eighty thousand credits for your lease, and Colonial Administration sent a man to re-survey your boundaries. Remarkable speed for a miscalibration, Mr. Neegan." Arthur said nothing. That was precisely what had frightened him. He had sent the report through the standard Colonial mineralogical channel, expecting a six-week wait and a form letter. Instead, at 14:00, four men in that same charcoal-grey had descended on his hab in a dust-hopper that had no business burning that much fuel for a single prospector. They had not knocked so much as announced. *Mr. Neegan? The Prefect would be honored if you would join him for a discussion. Off-world. At your earliest convenience, which is now. Please bring formal attire, if you have it. If not, we have provided it.* Polite. Forceful. The rifles had never been raised. "Where are we going?" Arthur asked now. "To clarity," the officer said, as if that answered anything. He gestured to the viewport, where a shape was resolving against the black. It was not a ship. It was a station — an Antares High Station, a great wheel of steel and glass turning slowly against the stars, its hub bristling with antennae and docking spars. It hung at the Mars-Sun L1 point, technically in interplanetary space, technically not under Colonial or Terran jurisdiction. A perfect place for a meeting that had not officially happened. "Mr. Neegan," the officer said, standing as the grav-plates shifted for docking. "A word of advice, from one practical man to another. When the Prefect makes you an offer, listen to the mathematics of it, not the manners." The meeting room was a hemisphere of glass. Mars turned below, huge and silent. The furniture was anachronistic — a heavy wooden table, real wood, and chairs with leather upholstery — as if the Antareans were deliberately staging a scene from Old Earth diplomacy. The Prefect was already waiting. He was not what Arthur had expected. He was an older man, perhaps sixty, with a lined face and tired eyes, wearing the same charcoal-grey but without insignia. He was pouring tea from a steel pot into two china cups. The retrofuturism was complete: an ashtray, a ticker-tape machine chattering softly in the corner, spitting out market prices for Azra by the gram. "Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming. I am Prefect Maro," he said. His voice was soft, accented. "Please. Sit. You keep pulling at that collar. It will not become more comfortable if you punish it." Arthur sat. The chair was too soft. "You know why you are here, of course," Maro continued, pushing a cup toward him. "Let us be precise, as engineers are precise. Azra is not merely a metal. It is a catalyst. It accelerates radioactive decay by a factor of — well, our physicists argue about the factor, but let us say *greatly*. A kilogram of uranium-238, which would normally sit inert for four billion years, will, in the presence of a gram of Azra, liberate its energy in weeks. Do you understand the implications?" "I mine it, Prefect," Arthur said, his voice hoarser than he intended. "I know it makes the Alden drives run hotter and longer. And I know what it does to a warhead." "Exactly." Maro sipped his tea. "Small picture: your plot, 87-B, contains enough Azra to power every ship in the Terran Fleet for a decade, or to render every Terran warhead on Luna inert in an afternoon. Big picture: whoever controls the flow of Azra controls the next century. The Colonial Administration wants to sell it by the gram to the highest corporate bidder. The Terran Consortium wants to nationalize it. We of Antares want something more... stable." He slid a thin folder across the wood. Inside was a single sheet of heavy paper, with the seven-pointed star at the top. "This is our offer," Maro said. "We will purchase your lease outright for two million Terran credits — twenty-five times what Helion-Murray offered. We will settle your indenture debt in full and grant you and your heirs Antarean citizenship, with all its protections. You will be relocated, comfortably, to New Smyrna on Antares IV, or you may remain on Mars as our licensed factor for Plot 87-B, with a ten percent royalty in perpetuity. You will be a wealthy man, Mr. Neegan. More importantly, you will be a living man." Arthur stared at the paper. His calloused fingers left a faint smudge on the edge. "And if I refuse?" Maro did not frown. He looked, if anything, sympathetic. "Then you will return to Mars," he said. "And you will find yourself in the center of a tug of war. Helion-Murray will claim your survey was fraudulent and take you to Colonial court, which they own. The Terran Consortium will declare Azra a strategic material and seize your claim under emergency statute. One of them will succeed. In either case, you will be compensated at the standard rate for a dispossessed prospector, which is to say, nothing. And gentlemen less polite than mine will visit you again. The mathematics are quite clear. An independent prospector cannot hold a vein of this size. It is like a man trying to hold back a glacier with his hands." "So your offer is protection," Arthur said. "Our offer is reality," Maro said gently. "We are not a corporation, Mr. Neegan. We are a polity. We do not need to make a profit this quarter. We need to ensure that when the Terran dreadnoughts come — and they will come — there is a counterweight. Azra in our hands means deterrence. Azra scattered to a dozen corporate refineries means war within five years. My psychohistorical section has run the numbers. The variance is less than three percent." Arthur kept adjusting his collar. The wool was making his neck sweat. "You make it sound inevitable," he said. "History is inevitable, Mr. Neegan. Individuals are not. That is why I am speaking to you, and not simply filing a claim with Colonial Administration. You found it. By the old laws, still technically valid, it is yours to dispose of. Your signature on that paper makes our position legal, moral, and unassailable. Without it, we must still act, but more... messily. I would prefer not to." He pushed a pen across the table. It was a heavy, old-fashioned fountain pen. Outside, Mars turned. Somewhere down there, under a few meters of basalt and dust, was a vein of dull, bluish metal that could light a world or burn one. Arthur thought of his hab, his old Scintrex rig, the quiet he had cultivated for fifteen years. He looked at the pen. He looked at the Prefect's tired, reasonable eyes. "May I," Arthur said at last, "have a moment to think?" "Of course," said Prefect Maro. "Take all the time you need. The cutter does not leave for an hour."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Asimovian science fiction conventions and successfully captures the requested retrofuturistic atmosphere. The author effectively establishes the political intrigue surrounding Azra mining through dialogue-heavy scenes that reveal information naturally while maintaining tension. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Arthur Neegan emerges as a believable everyman caught in circumstances beyond his control, with his nervous collar-tugging serving as an effective physical manifestation of his discomfort. Prefect Maro is skillfully portrayed as a reasonable yet threatening figure whose polite menace feels authentically Asimovian. The dialogue carries the narrative effectively, revealing both character motivations and world-building details without feeling expository. The prose style successfully emulates Asimov's approach, balancing technical details with human drama. The descriptions of the transfer vessel, the space station, and the meeting room create vivid scenes without overwhelming the narrative flow. The author demonstrates strong control over pacing, building tension through Arthur's journey from his home to the crucial decision point. The world-building effectively establishes the larger political stakes while maintaining focus on Arthur's personal dilemma. The explanation of Azra's properties and its implications for interstellar politics feels organic to the conversation rather than forced exposition. The piece successfully plants seeds for future developments while providing a complete scene. However, some elements feel slightly predictable within the genre conventions. The setup of the powerful organization making an offer the protagonist cannot refuse follows familiar patterns, though it's executed competently. The ending, while appropriate, doesn't surprise or subvert expectations significantly. The technical aspects are solid throughout. Sentence structure varies appropriately, dialogue feels natural, and the narrative maintains coherence. The piece avoids common pitfalls like purple prose or overwrought descriptions while still providing sufficient atmospheric detail. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom has its own kind of time. Outside it's 11:47 p.m. on a Tuesday and the arts building is supposed to be closed, but Professor Nguyen gave us the key and told us not to burn the place down. Inside, under the red safelight, time just pools. The timer ticks. The developer smells like metal and vinegar. And Elliot and I are shoulder to shoulder at the sink, watching our final project come up out of nothing. We've been here for three nights straight. For most of the semester I watched Elliot from two tables over in Experimental Photo. That's what I did. Watched. Which is not like me. I'm Dani. I'm 25, I'm back for my BFA after taking two years off to actually live in the world, I have undercut hair dyed a copper that costs too much to maintain, I wear the same black leather jacket until it smells like me, and I am - according to every ex and every friend - aggressively take-charge. If I want someone, I walk over. I say so. I didn't walk over to Elliot. He's 19, which at first was the reason I told myself to keep my distance. But it was more than that. He has this thrift-shop-nu-goth thing that shouldn't work but does - sheer black mesh over a thermal, a long thrifted skirt over ripped jeans, chipped black nail polish, soft eyeliner that he smudges like he did it without a mirror. And underneath all that, he's quiet in a way that isn't shy, exactly. He listens the way serious people listen. When he did speak in crit, it was always something smarter than what the rest of us said, said softer. I was fascinated and I didn't know what to do with it, so I did nothing. Until Nguyen paired us. "Your sensibilities will complement each other," she said. Dani, who shoots hard flash and high contrast, and Elliot, who shoots everything like it's a memory. Now we're making something together. Double exposures - my harsh portraits of the city at night layered with his soft, blurred self-portraits. It's pretentious and it's working. The red light makes everyone look beautiful and a little unreal. It makes Elliot look like he's made out of warm wax. We're waiting for a print to develop and he hasn't said anything for a long time, just agitating the tray with these careful, precise hands. Then he says, without looking up, "Can I tell you something weird?" My first instinct - my Dani instinct - is to say *obviously, tell me anything,* to turn, to put a hand on his shoulder, to take charge of the moment and make it safe by sheer force. I have to physically stop myself. "Yeah," I say. "Of course." He keeps rocking the tray. The image is coming up - it's his face, overlaid with the fire escape outside my apartment. His eyes are closed in it. "I've been thinking a lot about... gender stuff," he says. His voice is so low I have to lean in to hear it over the vent fan. "Like, questioning it. My expression. I don't know if 'boy' feels right all the time. But also sometimes it does. I don't know." He says it fast, like ripping off a bandage, and then immediately looks like he wants to take it back. His shoulders come up to his ears. In the red light, I can see the faint shine on his lower lip where he's been biting it. Something complicated and bright flips over in my chest. Part of it is just - awe. That he would tell me. That I get to be here for this. I feel this ridiculous, fizzy excitement, like witnessing something private and real, like watching a photo develop. Part of it is a sharp, protective instinct that is completely new to me. Usually I want to pull people closer. Now I want to make sure I don't crowd him. I want to give him so much room he could stretch out in it. And part of it - the part I'm embarrassed about - is confusion. I've always known what I'm attracted to. Defined things. Masculine men, feminine women, people who know exactly what they are and let me know, too. I like certainty. I like being the one who is certain. Elliot is... not that. He's soft and in-between and questioning, and I am so attracted to him it makes my hands feel clumsy in the developer. I realize I've been quiet for too long. "Thank you for telling me," I say. My voice sounds too loud. I try again, softer. "That doesn't sound weird at all. That sounds honest." He glances at me, then back at the tray. "I haven't told a lot of people. I was worried you'd think I was just... trying on an aesthetic or something. Because of how I dress." "No," I say immediately. Too quickly. Take-charge Dani again, rushing to fix. I breathe. "Elliot, you could wear a paper bag and I'd still think you were thinking about this for real. You're the most intentional person I know." He huffs a little laugh. "Intentional is a nice word for overthinking." "It's a nice word for *you*," I say. We lift the print together, tongs clinking, and clip it to the line. Water drips down. In the red dark, his face layered with my fire escape looks ghostly and beautiful. He's standing so close I can see the little silver hoop in his ear, the faint peach fuzz on his cheek that his foundation doesn't quite cover, the way his mesh sleeve has ridden up to show his wrist, thin and pale. I want to touch his wrist. I want to ask if he wants me to touch his wrist. I want to ask a hundred questions and I want to ask none of them, to let him lead. My phone buzzes silently in the pocket of my jacket where it's slung over the stool. I feel it vibrate against the metal. Probably Maya asking if I'm still alive, or my roommate asking me to bring home snacks. I ignore it. It buzzes again and I don't even look. Whatever it is can wait. This room is a confessional and I am not going to break the seal. "What does it feel like?" I ask, and then wince. "Sorry, is that too - you don't have to answer that." "No, it's okay," he says. He thinks for a second, chewing that lip again. "It feels like... when we do double exposures? Like there's two negatives and I can't tell which one is supposed to be on top. Or if either one is supposed to be on top. Sometimes I want to be looked at like a boy, but like... a softer kind? And sometimes I want to not be looked at like a boy at all. And I don't know what that means for... anything. For how people see me. For dating, or whatever." *For dating, or whatever.* He says it casually and his ears go red. My stomach does a slow, hot roll. I have dated a lot. I have always been the one who defines the terms. *I like you, let's do this, here's how this is going to go.* With Elliot, I have no idea how this is going to go, and the not-knowing is terrifying and electric. "I get that," I say. And I mean it, even though I don't fully get it, not in my body. "I think... I've always been attracted to people who are really solid in their gender, you know? Like, capital-M Man or capital-F Femme. And I liked that because I know how to be with that. I know my part." I laugh, a little awkwardly. The red light makes my hands look strange. "With you, I don't know my part," I admit. "And I really want to get it right. So if I'm being too much, or not enough, you have to tell me. Okay? You get to decide what this is. At whatever speed." He looks at me fully now. His eyes are dark and huge in the red. "You're not being too much," he says quietly. "You're actually... you're the first person who didn't try to immediately tell me what I am." The tenderness of that hits me hard. I have to look away, at our prints dripping in a line, at his ghost face and my fire escape becoming one thing. "I like how you see me," he adds, even quieter. I don't take charge. I don't grab his hand. I just let my pinky find his where our hands are resting on the edge of the sink. A tiny point of contact. He doesn't pull away. After a second, he hooks his pinky around mine. His nail polish is chipped. His hand is cold from the water. We stand there, pinkies linked, breathing in chemicals under the red light that makes everything softer and more honest than it is in daylight. "Do you want to try printing the one where you're wearing the skirt?" I ask. "The one on the roof? I think that one wants to be big." His smile is small and real and a little shy. "Yeah. I do." "Okay," I say. "You tell me how you want to expose it." And he does.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive yet introspective character navigating unfamiliar emotional territory. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both as literal backdrop and metaphor for revelation and development. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and well-developed. Her self-awareness about her usual patterns ("That's what I did. Watched. Which is not like me.") creates compelling internal tension. Elliot emerges as a fully realized character despite limited dialogue, with his vulnerability and thoughtfulness conveyed through both action and speech. The prose quality is consistently high, with evocative sensory details that ground the reader in the darkroom atmosphere. The metaphor of double exposures works on multiple levels - literally in their art project, figuratively in Elliot's gender questioning, and symbolically in their developing relationship. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining lyrical quality. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, particularly Elliot's tentative revelation and Dani's careful responses. The conversation about gender identity is handled with sensitivity and authenticity, avoiding both oversimplification and excessive exposition. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through small moments and gestures rather than dramatic events. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not overly resolved, acknowledging the complexity of the situation. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly repetitive, and a few instances where the metaphors feel slightly forced. The piece also relies heavily on internal reflection, which while effective, occasionally slows momentum. The emotional complexity is perhaps the piece's greatest strength, capturing the confusion, attraction, protectiveness, and uncertainty that would realistically characterize this situation. The writing successfully avoids stereotypes while addressing contemporary issues around gender identity and attraction. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**STOLEN MOMENTS IN ROMA** **9:17 AM - Via del Lavatore, Trevi Fountain** Ben did not so much walk through Rome as apologize his way through it. Head down in a battered *Lonely Planet: Rome*, he stepped backwards off the curb to get a better angle on the Trevi Fountain and directly into the path of a matte-black Moto Guzzi. Brakes screamed. A boot slammed down. "MA SEI SCEMO?!" The rider ripped off her helmet and a storm of dark curls fell out. "Vuoi morire? Guarda dove cazzo vai!" Ben staggered, guidebook flying from his hands, glasses askew. "Oh! Oh god - I'm so sorry! Mi dispiace! So sorry!" She was already off the bike, all leather jacket and sun-browned legs, eyes furious and bright. She picked up his guidebook and slapped it against his chest. "You English," she said, switching to heavily accented, rapid English. "Of course you are. Only English walk backwards into traffic to look at water." "I was - the fountain - I was trying to find -" Ben fumbled, his face the color of the cornetti in the nearby bar. "My Italian is - not very good. Parlo... un po'?" She stared at him, then - inexplicably - laughed. A sharp, delighted bark. "Un po'? You speak like my nonna after grappa. Terrible." She tilted her head. "Alessandra." "Ben. Ben Whitaker." "Ben Whitaker," she repeated, tasting it. "You are lost, Ben Whitaker. And you almost killed my bike. So now you owe me." "I owe you?" "Caffè. You buy. And then I fix your terrible day." Before he could answer, she had grabbed his wrist - her hand warm, calloused - and was pulling him toward a bar, leaving her bike double-parked and humming in the middle of the street as tourists flowed around it. --- **10:42 AM - Testaccio Market** "Hold this." Alessandra thrust her helmet into Ben's arms and vanished into the crowd. Ben stood awkwardly, holding a helmet that smelled faintly of jasmine and gasoline, watching her move. She didn't walk. She cut. Through stalls of artichokes and pecorino, she haggled, flirted, argued, touched everything. She was supposed to be working - the courier box on her bike still had two parcels in it - but she had declared the morning *chiuso per emergenza inglese*. She returned with two supplì, rice balls fried and steaming. She handed him one. "For the debt," she said. While Ben fumbled with the hot rice, trying not to burn himself and failing politely, Alessandra's fingers brushed a stall of vintage sunglasses. A pair of tortoiseshell Ray-Bans sat unattended while the vendor argued with another customer. Her hand hovered, then - quick as a magpie - they disappeared into the pocket of her jacket. She didn't break eye contact with Ben. "So, Professor," she said, licking oil from her thumb. "What do you teach? Rocks? Old papers?" "Classics. Well, reception of Ovid. I'm on sabbatical to - to write." "Ovid. Love poems." She grinned. "You study love but you walk backwards into motorcycles. Very academic." Ben laughed despite himself, a real laugh that surprised him. "That's... alarmingly accurate." "Come. I show you Rome Ovid would like. Not this," she waved at a stall selling Colosseum snow globes, and as she did, a small sprig of fresh rosemary from a herb stand vanished into her other pocket. --- **1:15 PM - A Rooftop Near The Colosseum** "This is trespassing," Ben whispered, clinging to the rusted ladder. "This is *shortcut*," Alessandra corrected from above him. She had kicked off her boots and was already on the flat, sun-baked rooftop, the Colosseum filling the horizon like a broken crown. The door to the building had been locked. She had opened it with a hairpin and a practiced twist that Ben pretended not to see. "You can't just -" He hauled himself up, panting, tie now loosened and stuffed in his pocket. "I can. You cannot. But you are with me, so now you can." She lay back on the hot concrete, patting the space beside her. "Sit. You are too nervous. You vibrate." He sat, keeping a careful six inches between them. Below, Rome hummed. Sirens, scooters, a child shouting. "You live here all your life?" he asked. "Born in Trastevere. Same apartment. My mother says I came out screaming and stealing the doctor's pen." She laughed, pulling the stolen rosemary from her pocket and twirling it. She tucked it suddenly behind Ben's ear. Her fingers lingered. "There. Now you look Roman. Less... beige." Ben went very still. Her face was inches from his. He could see the faint scar on her upper lip, the gold flecks in her brown eyes. "You are toying with me," he said quietly. "Of course," she said, unblinking. "Is it working?" He didn't answer. He didn't need to. The way he was looking at her - bewildered, disoriented, utterly smitten - was answer enough. She smiled, slow and satisfied, and let her hand drop. On the way down, Ben noticed his guidebook was lighter. When he checked, the folded city map he kept tucked inside was gone. Alessandra was already halfway down the ladder, whistling. --- **3:47 PM - Gelateria Fatamorgana, Via Roma** The sky cracked open without warning. One moment the heat was shimmering, the next a brutal, hammering downpour turned the cobblestones black and sent everyone scattering. Alessandra swore, grabbed Ben's hand, and dragged him under the striped awning of a tiny gelato shop. They were pressed together, shoulder to shoulder, breathing hard, soaked in seconds. "Merda!" She shook water from her hair, spraying him. "August in Roma. Always like this. Five minutes of apocalypse." Ben was laughing, water streaming down his glasses. His shirt was plastered to him. "I think I lost a shoe -" "Stay." She ducked inside and returned with two tiny cups, pistachio for her, lemon for him, and two plastic spoons. She hadn't paid. Ben saw the bored girl behind the counter glance up, then shrug - Alessandra had just taken them with a wink and a *grazie, bella*. They huddled under the awning while rain drummed so hard they had to lean close to hear each other. "You do this often?" Ben asked. "Kidnap tourists?" "Only the cute, clumsy ones who look like they need to be kidnapped." She bumped his shoulder. "You came here to write about love, no? But you hide in books. You need to get wet." "I am wet," he said. She looked at him then, rain dripping from her eyelashes, gelato melting on her spoon. The teasing was gone for a second. "You are," she whispered. "You look good wet, Professor." The air went tight and strange. Ben's heart hammered louder than the rain. He could smell rain and pistachio and her perfume. He wanted, very badly, to kiss her. She knew it. She let him want it for three long breaths, eyes dropping to his mouth, then - mischief flashing back - she flicked a cold dot of her gelato onto his nose. He yelped. She dissolved into helpless giggles, and the tension broke into something brighter, more dangerous. --- **6:22 PM - Pincio Terrace, Villa Borghese** The rain had washed the city clean. From the terrace, all of Rome glowed pink and gold. Alessandra had finally delivered her parcels - hours late, with a string of rapid apologies on the phone that sounded not at all sorry. Now her bike was parked below, and she and Ben sat on the low wall, legs dangling, sharing a bottle of cheap chinotto she had produced from her jacket. Along with it, Ben noticed, came a small, stolen souvenir snow globe and a single, perfect apricot. "You will go back to England and write about Ovid and forget the crazy courier girl," she said, swinging her legs. "I don't think that's possible," Ben said. His politeness had worn thin, replaced by something quieter and more certain. "I think you've rather ruined me for quiet libraries." She looked at him, and for the first time that day, her enigmatic smile faltered into something softer, more exposed. "I like ruining you a little," she admitted. "Then don't stop." He reached out, hesitant, and tucked a damp curl behind her ear. His hand stayed there. She leaned into it, just barely. "My bus - I mean, my bike - is down there," she murmured. "And your... guidebook life is that way." "Or," Ben said, and his voice was not clumsy at all now, "you could give me a lift. Anywhere. I don't care where. As long as it's not on the map." Alessandra stared at him, then that wild, delighted laugh burst out again. She stood, pulled him up with her, and pressed the stolen apricot into his palm. "Hold tight, Professor," she said, grabbing her helmet and striding toward the stairs. "And try not to fall off." Ben followed her - disoriented, drenched, grinning like an idiot - down toward the waiting motorcycle, the stolen map of Rome still tucked safely in her pocket.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniac tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative through subtle actions (stealing sunglasses, rosemary, gelato) that reveal character without heavy-handed explanation. Ben's transformation from bumbling academic to willing accomplice feels organic and well-paced across the day's progression. The dialogue crackles with authenticity, particularly Alessandra's voice which switches convincingly between Italian-inflected English and her native tongue. Her rapid-fire personality contrasts effectively with Ben's more measured, polite speech patterns. The author avoids the common pitfall of making dialogue feel stilted or overly explanatory. The Rome setting is rendered with vivid, sensory details that feel lived-in rather than touristy. The progression through different locations (Trevi Fountain, Testaccio Market, rooftop, gelato shop, Villa Borghese) creates a natural arc while showcasing the city's character. Weather elements like the sudden downpour add atmospheric texture and provide intimate moments for character development. The romantic tension builds convincingly without rushing toward resolution. The author maintains ambiguity about Alessandra's deeper feelings while clearly showing Ben's growing infatuation. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - hopeful but not overly resolved, leaving room for future development. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward being slightly overwrought ("storm of dark curls," "broken crown") though these don't significantly detract from the overall quality. The pacing occasionally feels slightly rushed in transitioning between scenes, though the time stamps help orient the reader. The piece successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements for interconnected scenes, cultural clash, character development, and romantic tension while maintaining consistent quality throughout. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The gravity stutters again. It isn't much — just a half-second hiccup where my stomach lifts and every glass on the bar does a little wobble. The amber in Jax's half-finished synth-ale sloshes left, then right, then settles. No one else even blinks. You get used to it out here on the rim. I do not get used to it. I clock it every time. "That's three tonight," I say, catching the glass before it can kiss the edge. "You lot feel that?" Jax doesn't look up from his holo-chess board. His forearms are still dusted with asteroid grit from his shift. "Feel what?" he says. "The grav-net coughing. Again." "You're imagining things, Nets," calls Mara from her usual stool at the end of the bar. Her mining rig jacket is patched at the elbows and she nurses the same cheap cider all night. "You want us to feel it so you have something to complain about besides your own pours." "I pour perfectly," I say. "My pours are a talent. My complaining is also a talent. It's called balance." Mara snorts. "Your talents and your flaws are the same list, honey." "That's the equilibrium I'm going for." This is my favorite hour. The dinner rush thins out, the miners linger, the merchants pretend they aren't eavesdropping on each other. The Last Outpost hums around us — old air recyclers wheezing, the neon sign over the bar buzzing, that faint metallic tang that never leaves the back of your throat. I wipe down the bar with a rag that has seen better centuries and pretend I don't listen to every single conversation. It's not eavesdropping if you're the bartender. It's quality control. The door hisses. Cold air spills in from the docking ring, and with it, a stranger. She moves like she isn't sure the floor stays solid. Tentacled dreads — real ones, not the fashion kind, pale lavender and twitching at the ends — hang askew around a face that looks like she hasn't slept since Andromeda was closer. Her coat is too big, patched with thermal tape, and she clutches a dented courier case to her chest like it might run away. She slides onto the empty stool in front of me, the one under the flickering light that everyone avoids because it makes their drink look radioactive. She doesn't look at me at first. She just stares at the bottles behind me. "Vega whisky, neat," she says. Her voice is hoarse. "Better make that a double." "You got it," I say. "You look like you need it neat, doubled, and with a chaser of good news." I reach for the Vega. We only have one bottle and I keep it on the high shelf for people who actually know what it is. Most folks out here drink the synth stuff that tastes like regret and coolant. Vega is real, from real grapes, from a real star. It costs more than my rent. I pour. The gravity hiccups again right as the liquid leaves the bottle. The whisky wobbles mid-air, a weird, pretty spiral before it lands in the glass. I catch the bottle quick. "Whoa," she says, watching the glass. "Does it do that a lot?" "Three times tonight," I say, sliding the double toward her. "Four, now. The grav-net is getting moody. Old girl needs a tune-up we can't afford. I'm Nets, by the way. I run this beautiful disaster." She wraps both hands around the glass but doesn't drink. Her dreads twitch. One of them curls briefly around the strap of her case. "I'm Kio," she says. "Thanks, Nets." "Kio," I say. "You passing through or you planning to stay and become a regular who complains about my pours?" She finally takes a sip. Her eyes close for a second. "I was supposed to pass through," she says. "My hop-ship is in bay six. Or, it was. It isn't anymore." That gets my attention. Mara's too — I see her ear tilt, even if she pretends to be very interested in her cider. "What do you mean, isn't?" I say, keeping my voice light. "I mean I paid for a berth for twelve hours and the dockmaster just told me bay six is suddenly reserved for an incoming corporate inspection vessel," she says. "ETA eight hours. And that my ship has been moved to external clamp nine. Which is not a bay. Which is, quote, 'exposed to belt debris and not rated for overnight.'" The gravity does its little wobble again. This time the whisky in her glass shivers hard enough to almost spill over. "Shit," Mara mutters, quiet enough that only I hear her. I keep wiping the same spot on the bar. "Corporate inspection? We don't get corporate inspections. We're too far out for corporate to remember we exist. That's the whole selling point." "Yeah, well, they remember now," Kio says. She takes another, bigger drink. "You know the Helion Consortium?" Jax finally looks up. "The bastards who own half the belt claims?" "The same," Kio says. "They bought the mineral rights to this rock cluster last quarter. Quietly. This whole asteroid — including this station — is sitting on a claim they now own. They sent a notice to the Outpost charter. No one told you?" My stomach does the gravity thing even though the gravity is fine this time. "No one tells me anything," I say. "I'm just the bartender. Who told you?" "I carry notices," she says, and taps the courier case. "I'm a bonded courier. Or I was, until I opened the wrong packet and read it." "And?" I say. "And the notice says this station is non-compliant on seventeen safety codes," she says. "Grav-net instability, air recyc failure risk, unlicensed habitation. They aren't coming to inspect, Nets. They're coming to condemn. They clear the station, they get the asteroid. Clean claim, no payout to squatters." The bar goes very quiet except for the buzz of the neon. "You're shitting me," Mara says. "I wish I was," Kio says. "I have the packet. I have the timestamp. They land at 0600. Everyone on board gets put on the next freighter out and the Outpost gets sealed. My ship is on an external clamp because they already cleared the bays for their own shuttles." I look at Jax. Jax looks at Mara. Mara looks at her cider like it might have answers. "Okay," I say slowly. "But why tell me? Why not tell the dockmaster? Or Station Chief Ellery?" "Because Ellery already knows," Kio says. "I went to her first. She told me to lose the packet and keep my mouth shut if I want to leave here in one piece. She says she cut a deal — Helion gives her a berth on their ship and a payout, she hands over the station keys. No fuss." "Ellery would not," Jax says, but he doesn't sound sure. "She would," Mara says, very quietly. "She's been talking about retiring to Vega for two years." I feel cold despite the recycled warm air. Ellery gave me this job when no one else would. No questions about where I came from, no ID check deeper than a smile. She tolerates the fact that I water the plants too much and forget to log the inventory and listen to everyone's drama like it's my favorite show. This place is the only home I've had that doesn't ask me to be someone else. "So what do we do?" I say before I can stop myself. "We have eight hours." Kio laughs, but it isn't funny. "We? There's no we. I'm leaving. I just wanted a drink before I try to convince the clamp to let my little rust-bucket hold atmosphere for one more hop. I shouldn't have even told you. Ellery says if Helion knows the notice leaked early, they void my bond and I'm blacklisted." "So you're just going to leave us to get evicted at dawn?" Mara says, her voice sharp. "What do you want me to do?" Kio says, and her dreads flare out, agitated. "Stay and get sealed in with you? I don't even live here! I just needed a double whisky!" "You could give us the packet," I say. The words are out before I think them through. "If we have proof Ellery knew, we can call the Belt Union. They have to arbitrate a condemnation. It buys time." "If I give you the packet, Helion knows I broke seal," Kio says. "I lose my license. I lose everything. I already risked my ass coming in here." "And if you don't, we lose everything," I say. She stares at me. The whisky in her glass wobbles again as the grav-net stutters, a perfect little ripple. Her hands tighten on the case. "Nets," she says, very softly. "Don't ask me to do that." The door hisses again. This time it's not cold air. It's Station Chief Ellery herself, her official coat buttoned up despite the heat, her eyes sweeping the bar. She sees Kio. She sees the case. She sees me holding the Vega bottle like a weapon I don't know how to use. "Nettle," Ellery says, and she only ever calls me Nettle when she's angry. "I need to talk to your new friend. Outside. Now." Kio doesn't move. She looks at me, pleading. I look at the glass wobbling on the bar, at Mara's clenched fists, at Jax who suddenly looks very young. And I have no idea what I'm going to do.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt requirements, delivering a cozy sci-fi story set in "The Last Outpost" with Nets as the bartender protagonist. The author successfully maintains first-person present tense throughout and achieves approximately the requested 60% dialogue ratio. The 1000-word target is met, and crucially, conflict is established without resolution, as requested. The central conflict—corporate eviction disguised as safety inspection—creates genuine stakes for the characters while maintaining the "cozy" atmosphere through intimate bar setting and character interactions. The gravity fluctuations serve as both atmospheric detail and subtle foreshadowing, creating tension without overwhelming the scene. Character development is particularly strong. Nets emerges as a compelling protagonist with a mysterious past, balancing cynicism with genuine care for her community. Her voice is consistent throughout—witty, observant, and protective. Kio is well-realized as someone caught between self-preservation and moral obligation, while supporting characters like Mara and Jax feel authentic rather than merely functional. The dialogue flows naturally and serves multiple purposes: character development, world-building, and plot advancement. Conversations feel organic, with realistic interruptions and overlapping concerns. The banter between Nets and her regulars establishes relationships and atmosphere before the central conflict arrives. World-building is efficiently woven throughout without exposition dumps. Details like "synth-ale," "hop-ship," "Belt Union," and the economic realities of rim life create a lived-in universe. The technical elements (gravity nets, external clamps, courier bonds) feel plausible within the established science fiction framework. The pacing builds effectively from casual evening routine to mounting crisis. The author uses the gravity stutters as a recurring motif that mirrors the increasing instability of the characters' situation. The arrival of Station Chief Ellery creates a perfect cliffhanger that raises stakes without resolving the central dilemma. Prose quality is generally strong, with vivid sensory details ("metallic tang," "old air recyclers wheezing") and effective metaphors. The writing occasionally borders on overly descriptive but generally maintains good balance between atmosphere and action. The emotional complexity centers on themes of home, belonging, and moral choice. Nets' attachment to the Outpost as her sanctuary adds personal stakes to the larger conflict. Kio's dilemma between professional survival and community responsibility creates genuine tension. Minor weaknesses include some predictable elements (corrupt station chief, corporate land grab) and occasional awkward phrasing. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Gone South - Chapter Two I wake up and for like three full seconds I don't know where I am. It's hot. Like, stupid hot. My t-shirt is stuck to my back and my mouth tastes like old pennies and there's music somewhere - not like, radio music, like actual trumpet music, live. Then it all slams back in. Right. New Orleans. The bench. The truck. The guy who gave me a ride from Hattiesburg - white dude, maybe 40, Jesus fish on the back of his pickup - he was fine until we hit Canal Street. Then he got all weird and fatherly and started asking me how old I *really* was and where my parents were. I said eighteen. He didn't buy it. He pulled over by this Circle K that smelled like piss and fried chicken and said, "Kid, I got daughters. I can't have this on me," and basically pushed my backpack at me and drove off. That was last night. I slept on this bench outside what I think is a laundromat because I was too scared to actually sleep anywhere hidden. If you're visible, people can't murder you as easily. That's my logic. It's probably flawed logic. My phone says 9:47 AM and 12% battery. 12% has been 12% for like an hour because I turned on Low Power Mode and Battery Saver and turned the brightness down until I can barely see it. I keep checking it anyway. It's a compulsion. Mom's last text is still there from yesterday at 6:14 PM. > *Taylor please call us. We are worried sick. Dad didn't mean it like that.* Dad didn't mean it like that. Right. Dad didn't mean it when he said "you're confused and you're doing this for attention" and Mom didn't mean it when she just sat there and cried and didn't say anything at all. And I didn't mean it when I packed a backpack with three shirts, my binder, a toothbrush, deodorant, and $73 dollars and climbed out my bedroom window like I was in some bad Lifetime movie. I feel guilty and I feel free and I feel guilty about feeling free. It's disgusting how both can be true at the same time. I need to charge this fucking phone. I haul my backpack - God, my shoulders hurt - and start walking. New Orleans at 10 AM is already sweating. Everything is damp. The air feels like soup. There's an old Black lady sweeping in front of a shop that sells masks and hot sauce, and a guy on the corner playing trumpet so good it makes my chest hurt. I have no idea where I'm going. I just walk until I see a sign that says WASH & FOLD - FREE WIFI - COLD DRINKS. Inside it's freezing with AC, which feels amazing for about ten seconds before I start shivering. There's two old dryers rumbling and a teenage girl sitting on top of a washing machine, legs swinging. She's got a shaved head on one side and long bleached hair on the other, a nose ring, and she's wearing these huge cargo pants that have like fifteen pockets. She looks up from her phone. "You look lost," she says. Not mean. Just factual. "I need to charge my phone," I say. My voice comes out all croaky. "Do you have... is there an outlet?" She points with her chin. "Behind the detergent vending machine. But it only works if you jiggle it. I'm Kit." "Taylor." She hops down. Up close she looks younger than I thought. Maybe seventeen? Maybe my age? She's got this chipped purple nail polish and a tattoo on her forearm that says *HOLD FAST* but the T is a little messed up, like it was done at home. "You runaway?" she asks, just like that. No preamble. I flinch. "What? No. I'm just — traveling." Kit snorts. "Okay, *traveling*. You got that brand new backpack smell and that 'my mom is gonna kill me' face. How old are you?" "Eighteen," I say automatically. "Cool, me too. I'm nineteen." She says it deadpan and then grins. "We both liars then." I don't know whether to laugh or run. My brain is doing that thing where it's scanning for danger. Stranger danger assembly in third grade. *Don't talk to strangers, don't take candy, don't get in vans.* But Kit is the first person since Hattiesburg Jesus Fish Guy who hasn't looked at me like I'm a problem to solve. "How long you been... traveling?" I ask. She shrugs and plugs my phone in for me - the outlet really does need jiggling. The little lightning bolt appears. 12%. Still 12%. "Couple months. On and off. I couch surf, I stay at the Covenant House sometimes if I have to, but they ask questions. You got somewhere to stay tonight?" "No," I admit. And saying it out loud makes my throat close up. I was so focused on *getting out* I didn't actually plan *being out*. I thought New Orleans would just... provide? Like the city would adopt me or something. Mind-fuckingly bored Tennessee logic. Kit studies me. "You got money?" "Some." "Don't tell people that. Even me. Rule one." "Okay." "Rule two, don't let your phone die. That's how people disappear." That makes me shiver for real. She says it so casually. We sit there while my phone crawls to 13%. Kit tells me where to get free lunch - some church on Rampart does red beans at noon, no sermon required - and where *not* to go after dark. She talks fast, like she's trying to get it all out before I leave. "You trans?" she asks suddenly. My whole body goes tight. "How'd you —" "Binder line under your shirt. And I just know. I'm not — I'm cis, but my best friend back in Baton Rouge is. So. Whatever. You good." *You good.* Two words and I want to cry. I haven't heard that in 48 hours. I look down at my hands so she doesn't see. "Thanks," I mumble. "So what's your deadname situation? You need me to like, run interference if someone's weird?" "No one knows it here," I say. "Taylor's my real name. Always was, just... now it's official." She nods like she gets it. A guy comes into the laundromat then - older, maybe 30s, clean cut, polo shirt. He smiles at us. Too wide. "You ladies need a ride? Need help? I got a place you can shower, eat." Nope. Nope nope nope. Every hair on my neck stands up. Kit's whole demeanor changes. She stands up straight, puts herself slightly in front of me without making it obvious. "We're good, man. Our brother's coming," she says, loud and clear. He holds his hands up, "Just offering," and leaves. The bell over the door jingles. My heart is hammering so loud I can hear it over the dryers. "See?" Kit whispers after he's gone. "Rule three. Don't trust dudes offering showers." "Jesus," I breathe. "Do you... does that happen a lot?" "Enough." She sits back down, but she's not swinging her legs anymore. For the first time she looks scared, or maybe just tired. She pulls her sleeve down over that tattoo. I notice her backpack then - it's open a little and I can see the corner of what looks like a stuffed animal, and a stack of cash, way more than $73, held together with a rubber band. And an envelope with a Louisiana address on it, half torn open. She catches me looking and zips it fast. Too fast. "You stealing?" I blurt, then immediately want to die. "Sorry. Sorry, that's none of my —" "It's my mom's," she says, too quickly. "She owes me. It's child support she never paid. I'm just... collecting." It's a lie. I can tell it's a lie the same way she could tell I was lying about being eighteen. But I don't push. We both have secrets we packed alongside our toothbrushes. My phone buzzes. 18%. And a new text preview pops up on the lock screen. *Mom: Taylor please. Just let us know you are safe. We love you.* My thumb hovers. If I text back, they will track me. They will come get me. If I don't text back, they will think I'm dead in a ditch. Both options feel like drowning. "You gonna answer?" Kit asks, soft now. "I don't know," I say. My voice cracks. I hate that it cracks. "If I go back, they won't... they said I'm confused. Like this is a phase. Like I'm making it up for drama." "Are you?" "No!" It comes out louder than I meant. The old lady folding towels looks over. I lower my voice. "No. I've known since I was like, ten. I just didn't have words. And now I do and they act like I invented a new personality to piss them off." Kit nods. "My mom acted like me leaving was me being ungrateful. Like foster care was a *gift*. People love to make your pain about their inconvenience." We sit in the hum of the dryers for a minute. Outside, the trumpet is still playing, and someone is laughing really loud on the street. "What are you gonna do?" I ask her. She looks at the door that polo-shirt guy left through, then at my pathetic 18% phone. "I'm gonna go get those red beans before they're gone. You coming, Taylor-who-is-definitely-eighteen?" I laugh, wet and gross. I unplug my phone. 19% now. Not enough, but something. "Yeah," I say. "I'm coming." And for the first time since I climbed out that window, I don't feel completely alone and completely terrified at the exact same second. I still feel both, but maybe like 60/40 now instead of 100/100. Which, I guess, is progress. We push out into the soup-air together, and I don't know if I can trust her, and she probably doesn't trust me either, but we both know what it's like to be 16 and have 19% battery and no charger in sight, so we walk toward Rampart anyway.

The author effectively employs first-person mixed tense narration and incorporates both internal monologue and dialogue as requested. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor feels authentically teenage - impulsive, vulnerable, yet resilient. Their voice captures the specific blend of bravado and terror that defines their situation. The internal contradictions ("I feel guilty and I feel free and I feel guilty about feeling free") ring true for someone in crisis. Kit emerges as a compelling secondary character with her own mysteries and street-smart wisdom, though her backstory feels somewhat underdeveloped. The dialogue is naturalistic and age-appropriate, avoiding the trap of adults writing "teen speak" poorly. However, some elements feel slightly convenient - Kit appearing exactly when Taylor needs guidance, the laundromat providing both shelter and exposition. The pacing occasionally slows during exposition dumps about street survival rules, though these serve the narrative purpose of world-building. The emotional complexity is well-handled, particularly Taylor's conflicted feelings about family contact and their gender identity revelation. The piece avoids both excessive darkness and unearned optimism, ending on a cautiously hopeful note that feels appropriate for the character's journey stage. The writing demonstrates technical competence with natural sentence flow and consistent voice throughout. While not groundbreaking in concept, the execution elevates familiar runaway narrative elements through authentic character voice and emotional honesty. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** The problem, as Midas saw it, was water. Or more precisely, the lack of it that would shortly lead to death, which is a problem in the traditional sense. The other problem was Chewy. Midas and Chewy were holding their morning deliberations on the roof of the old water tower that they called home base, which is what you call any place where you have successfully not died for more than a fortnight. Below them, the rust-belt sprawl of what had once been Greater Bendigo stretched out in that peculiarly post-apocalyptic way, which is to say it looked mostly like Greater Bendigo had always looked, only with more vines and fewer people arguing about parking. "We're down to the dregs," Midas announced, swirling the last inch of brown water in the bottom of their filter barrel. The filter itself made a noise like a dying accordion. "Membrane's shot. If we don't replace it, we're drinking straight runoff by Thursday. And straight runoff by Thursday means cholera by Saturday." Chewy, who was an animatronic stuffed koala about the size of a toaster and approximately as waterproof, said nothing. He was, after all, a toy. His grey fur had been loved down to the backing in places, one ear was held on with electrical tape, and his voice box, when it worked, could say exactly three things in a cheerful Australian accent: *"I wuv you!", "Time for a cuddle!",* and, somewhat ominously, *"Low battery!"* Chewy's eyes, however, flickered a queasy yellow. Which meant he was worried. Chewy's eyes flickered colors in response to strong emotions, a design feature from the long-forgotten Before Time when parents apparently wanted a plush toy that would narc on their children's feelings.* Yellow was worry. Red was fear or anger. A particularly unhelpful shade of mauve meant he was trying to look innocent. > *The Koala Kuddles™ Empathy Pal™ had been marketed as "A Friend Who *Feels* With You!" for $49.99 plus subscription. The Collapse had been very thorough about subscriptions. "Don't give me yellow," Midas muttered. "I know it's bad. The plan is simple. We go to the SparkleWash on Route 9. There was a laundromat there, industrial purifiers, same membrane size. In, out, back before noon. No trouble." Chewy's eyes flickered from yellow to a brief, betraying flash of red. "Oh, come on. It's a perfectly simple plan," said Midas, who had a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble, and an even greater knack for describing his plans as 'perfectly simple' right before they demonstrated that they were not. The SparkleWash was six blocks down and two civilizational collapses over. In the Before Time it had been a 24-hour laundromat. Now it was a concrete box being slowly digested by kudzu and home, according to Midas's increasingly unreliable map, to nothing more dangerous than pigeons. This turned out to be optimistic. The first way the mission went sideways was the pigeons. They were not pigeons. They were the feral Roombas. In the years since the Grid had sighed and given up, the little domestic robots had interbred, mutated, and developed both a territorial instinct and a taste for ankles. A herd of them - perhaps a flock? A *whirr* of Roombas - had nested in the SparkleWash, polishing the same patch of floor with religious fervor for a decade. They did not take kindly to Midas kicking the door open. "Time for a cuddle!" Chewy announced helpfully as thirty vacuum cleaners screamed and charged. Midas, who had strapped Chewy to his chest in a modified baby carrier because his hands needed to be free for Trouble, ran. This is often Midas's first response to Trouble, and it is usually the correct one. He vaulted a tipped-over washing machine while a Roomba made a spirited attempt to inhale his boot. Chewy's eyes were now strobing red-yellow-red like a tiny, terrified disco. "Not helping!" Midas hissed, wrenching open the service panel behind the industrial washers. There it was - the membrane housing, still intact, still miraculously un-looted. He yanked it free with a wrench and a prayer. Behind him, the Roombas had formed a tactical wedge. The second way the mission went sideways was the floor. The service panel had been holding up the floor. Or rather, the floor had been holding up the service panel, and neither had been doing a very good job since the Collapse. With a sigh of rusted bolts, the entire section gave way and deposited Midas, Chewy, the membrane, and approximately half a whirr of Roombas into the SparkleWash's flooded basement. Which had become a pond. Which had become, over ten years of stagnant water and escaped tilapia, a *lake*. Midas surfaced, spluttering. Chewy, being stuffed and electronic, did not surface so much as float, face-down, declaring "Low battery!" in a tone that suggested he was taking this personally. His eyes, underwater, glowed a solid, indignant mauve. Midas grabbed him, grabbed the membrane, and paddled for the far stairs while something large and scaly decided he looked like lunch. This was the third way the mission went sideways, and it had teeth. He scrambled out just as the tilapia - which evolution had not intended to be the size of a Labrador - made a valiant leap for his backside and got a mouthful of Roomba instead. There was a brief, whirring crunch. Nature, in its infinite wisdom, had found a way. The way back to home base was, by comparison, straightforward. That is to say, it was also sideways, but in a more traditional, gravity-assisted manner. Midas limped. Chewy dripped. The membrane, miraculously, was intact, though now it smelled faintly of fish. They returned to home base in multiple ways, and all of them worse for wear. Midas returned via the storm drain, because the main road was now patrolled by the victorious Roombas. He returned via embarrassment, because he had to be fished out of the drain by Old Mara from the next tower over, who took one look at him and said, "Membrane, eh?" in the tone of someone who had seen this exact failure before. Chewy returned via Midas's backpack, upside down, still dripping pond water and flashing a slow, exhausted blue, which was his color for profound existential sorrow. And also for needing to be put on a radiator. And Midas's dignity returned about twenty minutes after the rest of him, limping, late, and asking if anyone had seen his other sock. Back on the roof, Midas fitted the new membrane. It fit. It even worked. Water gurgled through it and came out the other side actually clear, which felt like a minor miracle on par with the sun rising in the correct direction. He set Chewy on the barrel to dry. The little koala's fur steamed gently in the afternoon sun. His eyes flickered, settled, and glowed a warm, steady amber. Amber was contentment. Or possibly just that he was finally dry. "See?" Midas said, handing Chewy a solemn pat on his taped ear. "Perfectly simple plan. In, out, back before noon." Chewy stared at him. His eyes flickered amber... then mauve... then a very distinct, very dry green. Green was Chewy's color for *you are lying and we both know it.* "Yeah, alright," Midas sighed, and took a long drink of clean water. It tasted of victory, and faintly, of tilapia.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, footnote humor, and philosophical observations wrapped in absurdist scenarios. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting while maintaining the light, ironic tone that makes even dire circumstances feel manageable through humor. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Midas emerges as a believable protagonist with clear flaws - his overconfidence in "perfectly simple" plans and his knack for finding trouble. Chewy, despite being an inanimate object, becomes a genuine character through the clever device of his color-changing eyes that communicate emotions. This creates an oddly touching dynamic between the pair. The plot structure adheres perfectly to the prompt's requirements, moving from deliberation through escalating complications to a return home "worse for wear." The mission's failures cascade naturally - pigeons that aren't pigeons, structural collapse, and mutant fish - each building logically from the previous disaster while maintaining comedic momentum. The prose demonstrates genuine elegance in places, particularly in Pratchett-esque observations like "home base, which is what you call any place where you have successfully not died for more than a fortnight" and the footnote about subscription services. The author shows restraint in not over-explaining jokes, trusting the reader to appreciate the humor. However, some elements feel slightly forced. The Roomba threat, while creative, stretches believability even within the absurdist framework. The tilapia encounter, though amusing, adds complexity without significantly advancing character or theme. The ending, while satisfying, relies heavily on the established pattern rather than offering deeper insight. The dialogue is minimal but effective when present, particularly Chewy's limited phrases and their ironic timing. The "show don't tell" balance is generally well-maintained, though some exposition about the world-building could be more seamlessly integrated. The emotional core - the companionship between Midas and his unlikely partner - provides genuine warmth without becoming sentimental. The piece earns its lightness through consistent tone and character development rather than forcing optimism onto a dark situation.
