+ Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Offworlder - Chapter 2: The Walk** I was twenty-four when the Ekumen sent me to Kethra, and I had been trained to be invisible. That is the first lesson of the envoy: to be a vessel, not a voice. My brief was simple and, as I now understand, entirely false. Kethra was settled in the first wave, eight hundred years ago. Two ships landed. One in the high basalt desert of the north, where the air is thin and the sun is merciless, and one in the deep, humid basin of the south. For eight centuries they did not meet. In that time humanity diverged, as it always does when left alone. The northern children grew tall and spare, their chests deep, their skin darkened to a matte black that drank the ultraviolet. They call themselves the Asten. The southern children grew short and broad, pale as river clay, with a second lid over the eye to keep out the damp and the spore. They call themselves the Tevar. Two subspecies, the briefing said, now forced back into contact by the need for water and lithium, and now on the brink of war. My job was to listen, to assess, to not take sides. The briefing documents used the word *tension* seventeen times. They included charts of resource distribution and photographs of the border wall that had been built around the northern aquifer. On my second day, they held a reception for me in the Administrative Compound. It was a white, climate-controlled building that could have been on Terra or Hain or any world that tries to forget what planet it is on. The Asten officials stood on one side of the room, the Tevar officials on the other. They did not speak to each other. They spoke to me, carefully, about grievances and histories, and I nodded and recorded and was, as instructed, invisible. The air recycling hummed too loud. I asked to be excused. Against protocol, I did not return to my quarters. The Compound has a side gate for service workers. No one stops a worker. I had studied the city maps; I knew the market was three blocks down, beyond the wall. I slipped the gate and went out alone, which an envoy is never supposed to do. The street outside was not in the briefing. The briefing had described a segregated city, a city of checkpoints. What I found was a street that was simply a street. Children were playing a game with stones in the dust. An old Asten woman, seven feet tall and thin as a reed, was haggling with a Tevar butcher, who was half her height and twice her width, over the price of smoked fish. They argued without rancor, in the rapid, clipped Kethran that my implant was still learning to parse. She laughed — a great, dry sound — and he laughed, and he wrapped the fish for her. No one looked at me at first. I was another offworlder, another pale, unadapted thing in a dull grey Ekumen tunic. Then a child stared openly at my eyes, which have no second lid, and I realized I was the strange one. The market opened before me without a wall or a gate. It was a square of packed earth, shaded by canvas awnings that snapped in the wind off the plateau. The smell was of roasting peppers, of oil, of dust. Market stalls sell handwoven fabrics dyed in pigments not found on Earth — a deep, light-drinking violet made from the basin lichen, a yellow so pale it seemed to be made of the thin northern air itself. An Asten weaver, her long fingers working a loom strung between two poles, was selling to a Tevar mother, who held the cloth up to her child's cheek to test its softness. Beside them, a Tevar man sold water in clay jars, and his best customers were Asten, who need more water in the thin air and who paid him not with money but with woven baskets. I had been told the Asten controlled the water and refused to share it. I had been told the Tevar controlled the looms and refused to trade. I bought a strip of the violet cloth for a coin I did not understand the value of. The weaver pressed it into my hands and said something my implant rendered as, "For the cold you carry with you." I did not know what she meant, but I kept it. I walked for an hour. I saw no wall. I saw Asten and Tevar mending a roof together, their different bodies making them good at different parts of the work — one reaching, one lifting. I saw them sharing shade. The social structure was not the one in my charts. It was not two nations in one city. It was a city that had learned, in the way cities do, to make use of its differences. When I returned, Command was waiting. My quarters are a single white room with an ansible link. The light was blinking red, which means a recorded reprimand, which is worse than a live one because it has been considered. Envoy Tali, the message said in the flat voice of my superior on the orbiter. You left the Compound without escort. You violated Article Four of Contact Protocol. You have endangered the mission and yourself. Do you understand that your perceptions are untrained and your conclusions premature? I stood with the dust still on my boots and the strip of violet cloth in my fist. The message continued. You will rectify this error by presenting yourself to the Minister of Science tomorrow morning at 08:00. He has requested an interview. Do not deviate again. The Minister of Science on Kethra is not a scientist. This I had been told. It is a political posting, given to the faction currently out of favor, a place to store an ambitious person where they can do little harm. The current Minister was an Asten named Varve. He was seventy years old and had survived three administrations. His office was not in the Compound. It was in the market district, above a grain store. I was escorted this time, by two unsmiling Tevar guards who left me at the door. Varve was very tall, even for an Asten. He had to duck his head under the doorway. His skin was the matte black of his people, but his hair had gone grey-white. He did not stand when I entered. He was shelling beans into a wooden bowl. He gestured for me to sit on a stool that was too low for me. "So," he said in perfectly clear Terran, without needing my implant. "The offworlder who goes for walks. Command is angry with you." "I am angry with Command," I said, before I could be invisible. He smiled. He pushed the bowl of beans toward me. "Shell," he said. It was not a request. I shelled beans. My hands are clumsy. "Tell me what you saw," he said. I told him about the market, about the weaver and the butcher, about the roof. I told him that his city did not match my briefing. "And what did your briefing tell you?" he asked. "That your peoples are divided. That you are close to violence over resources." He nodded slowly. "And what does an envoy do about violence?" "Prevent it," I said. "Mediate." "Ah." He picked up a bean and examined it. "We have a saying here. 'When the offworlder comes to save you, hide your water and hide your daughters.' Do you know why we built the wall around the aquifer, Envoy Tali?" "To keep the Tevar out," I said, repeating the briefing. "No. We built it because your people told us to. Your Ekumen, your Command, when they came last time, they said: 'You have two peoples, you must have a border. You must have a treaty about water.' So we built a wall to please you. And then we made a gate in it where no offworlder looks, and we carry the water through every morning. Tell me, should I show you the gate?" My hands stopped. "If I show you, you will report it," he said. "And Command will say we are deceitful. If I do not show you, you will report that we are divided, and Command will send mediators and resource managers and peacekeepers, and they will manage us until we are divided in truth. So, Envoy. What will you report?" He was not testing my knowledge. He was testing my will — whether I could hold a contradiction without needing to resolve it for my superiors. Whether I could be a vessel that does not immediately pour out what it contains. I thought of the violet cloth in my pocket. For the cold you carry with you. "I will report that the wall exists," I said at last. "And that the market exists. I will report that I do not yet understand which one is the city." Varve looked at me for a long time. Then he laughed, the same dry laugh as the old woman with the fish. "Good," he said. "You may be useful after all. Shell the rest of these beans. And tomorrow, go for another walk. But this time, tell Command you are going."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Ursula K. Le Guin's distinctive style and thematic preoccupations. The author successfully captures Le Guin's anthropological approach to science fiction, her interest in cultural misunderstanding, and her characteristic prose rhythm. The first-person narration mirrors Le Guin's frequent use of envoy protagonists, and the philosophical underpinnings about cultural perception versus reality are authentically rendered. The world-building is economical yet vivid, establishing the divergent human subspecies through physical description rather than exposition. The Asten and Tevar are believably differentiated by their environmental adaptations, and their market interactions feel organic rather than forced. The central conceit—that the apparent division is a performance for offworld observers—is both clever and thematically resonant with Le Guin's work on cultural imperialism. The protagonist's character arc is well-constructed, moving from dutiful invisibility to active questioning without feeling rushed. Tali's decision to venture into the market feels motivated by genuine curiosity rather than plot convenience. The progression from naive acceptance of briefings to recognition of deeper complexities mirrors the reader's journey. The dialogue, particularly with Minister Varve, crackles with intelligence and political sophistication. Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter 7: Polymerase Chain Reaction** Glow-in-the-dark mushrooms sprout in cracked lab tiles, remnants of old splicing tests. I leave them alone. They were an accident three winters ago when I tried to splice a bioluminescent marker from a jellyfish plasmid into oyster mycelium to make a living contamination sensor. The sensor worked. So did the mycelium. It ate through the agar, through the grout, and now it fruits every time the humidity spikes, little pale caps that throw a sick green light across the floor at night. Free light is free light. My lab is an old high-school biology room on the third floor of the Warren. The settlement below farms the parking lot. The windows are still taped with blackout film from when AgriGen's drones used to scan for unlicensed chlorophyll. The thermocycler clicks. It's not a thermocycler. Not anymore. It's a Zojirushi rice cooker with its guts ripped out and rewired to an Arduino taped to the side with yellowing surgical tape. I salvaged the heating block from a dead PCR machine in the university ruins, but the lid doesn't seal right so I weigh it down with a brick. It runs off a car battery that I charge with a bike generator. When it cycles, it shudders and smells faintly of burnt rice. 95 degrees. Denature. 55 degrees. Anneal. 72 degrees. Extend. Thirty times to make something out of almost nothing. The contract is sweating on my bench. The woman who brought it calls herself Varro. She came up the stairwell with a respirator and a sidearm and no settlement patch, which means Night Market. She didn't take her gloves off. She set a vacuum-sealed Mylar packet on my bench next to the brick-weighted rice cooker. Inside was maybe twenty grams of soybeans. They looked wrong — too uniform, too pale, like pearls. Generation Zero. "AgriGen GoldLine 8," she said. "Pre-Collapse vault stock. Still has the terminator intact." I knew what that meant. Before the grid died, before the blight and the burn, the corps solved hunger the way they solved everything else: subscription model. All the calorie crops — GoldLine corn, GoldLine soy, GoldLine wheat — were engineered with built-in obsolescence. The DNA lasted one generation. You planted, you harvested, but the seeds your harvest made were sterile, their chromosomes laced with methylated kill-switches and uracil-loaded telomeres that degraded like wet paper. You had to buy again next year. It maximized profits right up until the supply chains snapped and the buying stopped, and then it just maximized starvation. Every seed we grow now is a salvage job. We get second-gen grain that sprouts at 30% if we're lucky, and the seedlings come up stunted, leaves curled, already half-dead from their own suicide genes. My job for the Warren is to cut that kill-switch out. To splice in something that will actually breed true. "You want me to break terminator," I said. "I want you to make it *viable*," Varro said. "Ten kilos of fertile seed by spring. Enough to plant a field that plants itself next year. My buyer has land in the Basin." "My settlement needs that work. We're on ration." "Your settlement pays you in turnips." She slid a second thing across the bench. A cryo-vial, frosted, with a real medical seal. Inside, clear liquid. "Uncut insulin. Pre-Collapse, lab-made, not your yeast-piss homebrew. Six months' supply." My hand went to my side without thinking. Three years ago I got a gut infection from a bad batch of reclaimed water. No antibiotics. I had a CRISPR kit, a half-translated AgriGen veterinary manual, and a plasmid for a broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptide derived from horseshoe crabs. I cooked it in the rice cooker and shot it into my thigh with a jet injector I made from a pressure washer. It cured the infection. It also rewrote a few other things. The peptide never turned off. My sweat now smells faintly of brine and copper. The capillaries in my forearms are too visible, dark blue-green, and if I stay in the sun too long my skin prickles and flushes — not sunburn, *photosynthesis*. I have faint chlorophyll freckles across my shoulders that I cover with long sleeves. The physical toll is a constant low-grade tremor in my hands, a liver that aches when I drink, and a menstrual cycle that stopped completely. The unexpected upside: I haven't had a cold since. Cuts close in a day. And I can see perfectly in the dark. My eyes picked up the tapetum lucidum from the same plasmid — at night the mushroom light is bright enough to read by. Varro noticed me looking at the vial and smiled behind her mask. "You're crashing, biohacker. Your pancreas is editing itself to death. You keep making your own insulin with that dirty yeast vector, you're going to go autoimmune in a year." She wasn't wrong. My last batch of islet-patch yeast had given me hives for a week. The GoldLine soy in the packet is degrading as we speak. Vault stock or not, the uracil rot is ticking. In another forty-eight hours the DNA will be too fragmented to amplify. That's the cruelty of the design — even the seeds they locked away were designed to fall apart. So I have to run PCR now. I cut the Mylar with sterilized shears and pick out three beans. I grind them in a mortar I made from a car piston, add lysis buffer I brew from dish soap and pineapple enzymes, and spin it in the centrifuge — a Dremel tool bolted to a salad spinner, screaming at 10,000 RPM, held together with zip ties and prayer. The pellet at the bottom is barely there. I pipette it with a micropipette whose plunger I replaced with a 3D-printed thumb piece that sticks every third push. Into the PCR tubes go the primers. I designed them two years ago to flank the terminator cassette: a 2.1 kilobase stretch that codes for a lethal ribonuclease that activates in the embryo. If I can amplify the regions *around* it, I can use Gibson assembly to stitch the soy genome back together without the poison pill, and splice in a hardier promoter from wild river soy that actually knows how to make a seed that lives. The rice cooker clicks to 95. Denature. The double helix splits open. On the bench, my gel electrophoresis rig hums — a phone charger power supply, two graphite pencils for electrodes, agar I make from seaweed boiled off the roof collectors. It works. Varro watches. "You ever think about fixing yourself?" she asks, nodding at my hands. The tremor is bad tonight. "Every time I fix something, something else breaks," I say. "That's the rule with untested mods. You don't get a clean edit. You get a trade." "But you can see in the dark now." "And I can't have kids. Trade." The cooker clicks to 55. Anneal. Primers finding their home. If I give Varro ten kilos of fertile GoldLine, the Basin buyer will have the first truly open-pollinating crop in twenty years. They could feed a thousand people. They could also sell it, or weaponize it, or get drone-struck by whatever's left of AgriGen's IP enforcement. And the Warren, my Warren, will go into spring with the same stunted, half-sterile corn we've been nursing, because I only have enough wild soy promoter for one big edit this season. I can't do both. The cooker clicks to 72. Extend. Polymerase building. Varro taps the insulin vial. "You have twelve hours before that template is soup. Decide if you want to live to see your mushrooms fruit again." The brick on the rice cooker rattles. The mushrooms in the cracked tiles glow a little brighter, as if listening. In the green light, my green-veined hands look like they belong to something else — something that was designed to last more than one generation. I pull the next set of tubes from the ice bucket. "I'm going to need more Mylar," I say.

However, the dialogue feels somewhat functional rather than distinctive - Varro's speech patterns don't strongly differentiate her from the protagonist's internal voice.
